l: battle against Cendebaeus, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: A battle across a brook in the plain: John leads twenty thousand men and cavalry from Modin against Cendebaeus's large force, crosses first and rallies the fearful. At the trumpets the enemy flees; John pursues to Kidron, burns Azotus's towers, and about two thousand fall.

l: banquet and murder of Simon, The First Book of the Maccabees
s: Treacherous murder of Simon at Dok in Sebat, year 177: Ptolemy welcomed Simon and sons Mattathias and Judas into his stronghold, held a banquet with hidden men, then killed them and servants once drunk; condemned as evil repaid for good.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The Second Book of the Maccabees opens with two letters from the Jews of Jerusalem and Judea to the Jews of Egypt, urging them to keep the feast marking the temple's purification. The letters recall the hidden altar fire, later found as a liquid called Nephthar, and Jeremiah's hiding of the tabernacle, ark and incense altar. An abridger then explains that he is condensing Jason of Cyrene's five books on Judas Maccabaeus, the temple's purification, and the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and Eupator. The narrative begins in a peaceful Jerusalem under the godly high priest Onias. Simon's quarrel with Onias leads King Seleucus to send Heliodorus to seize the temple treasury, but heavenly figures scourge him to the ground. Under Antiochus Epiphanes the priesthood is bought by Jason and then by Menelaus, who has Onias murdered, and Greek customs spread. Antiochus invades Jerusalem, plunders the temple, and later forces the Jews to abandon their laws, renaming the sanctuary for Olympian Zeus. The narrator treats this as God's chastening. Eleazer, a ninety-year-old scribe, and seven brothers with their mother die rather than eat swine's flesh, declaring their hope in resurrection. Judas Maccabaeus then gathers faithful Jews and, with his brothers, defeats Nicanor, Timotheus and Bacchides. Antiochus, struck by an incurable illness, repents, vows to become a Jew, and dies in a strange land. Judas recovers and rededicates the temple on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, founding an eight-day festival. Under Antiochus Eupator, Lysias leads a vast army, but a heavenly horseman aids the Jews and Lysias sues for peace; letters from the king and Roman ambassadors confirm Jewish rights. Fighting continues with neighbouring peoples. After one battle Judas sends two thousand drachmas to Jerusalem for a sin offering, linked to belief in the resurrection. Eupator marches again with Lysias and Menelaus, who is put to death, and makes peace with the Jews. In the closing chapters Demetrius takes the country, and Alcimus accuses Judas. Demetrius sends Nicanor, who first befriends Judas, then turns hostile and threatens to level the temple. The elder Razis dies rather than be captured. Nicanor plans to attack on the Sabbath, but Judas, encouraged by a dream of Onias and Jeremiah, prays for a good angel and routs the army. Nicanor is found dead, and his head and arm are displayed in Jerusalem. The people decree the thirteenth of Adar a day of honor, and the author ends with remarks on his style.

l: Jews in Jerusalem and Judea, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: sends_greetings_to Jews in Egypt [letter author] They send greetings and a letter to the Jews in Egypt, together with the senate and Judas, addressed also to Aristobulus. They pray for the Egyptian Jews, recall their own suffering and prayers being heard, thank God for deliverance, and urge them to keep the feast of tabernacles in Chislev in the 188th year.

l: Jews in Egypt, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: located_in Egypt [throughout] They are the recipients of the letter from Jerusalem and Judea, which includes Aristobulus, King Ptolemy's teacher, of the stock of the anointed priests. They are prayed for and told to keep the feast of tabernacles in the month Chislev and to remember the fire given in Nehemiah's time.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: God, as presented in The Second Book of the Maccabees, is the Almighty Lord, Creator, and King of the world, called Sovereign of spirits and of all authority, King of kings, Lord of the universe who needs nothing, and the living Sovereign in heaven. He is the God of Israel, bound by covenant to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he dwells in heaven while watching over his habitation, the Jerusalem temple. The records stress that he is all-seeing, a righteous Judge who reveals hidden things, merciful, a worker of wonders, and one who always fights on the side of the Jews. He does not forsake them: he chastens his people promptly for their sins so that he never withdraws his mercy, and his anger turns to reconciliation with his servants. The account unfolds as a series of prayers and interventions. At the start he is asked to remember his covenant, and he is credited with hearing the Jews' prayers, saving them from great perils, and throwing their enemies out into Persia. He is said to have saved his people and restored the heritage, kingdom, priesthood, and consecration, and the writers hope he will gather them into his holy place. He protects the temple by felling Heliodorus, who then testifies that God dwells in heaven and strikes those who come to hurt the place. Under persecution, Eleazar and the martyred brothers and mother trust him to raise those who die for his laws to everlasting life and to punish their oppressors. Afterward he turns wrath to mercy, humbles Nicanor, strikes Antiochus with a fatal invisible stroke, and leads Maccabaeus and Judas to recover the temple and win victories over Timotheus, the Idumaeans, Gorgias, and others. A good angel and a white-clad horseman appear, and even Lysias concludes that the Almighty fought for the Hebrews. In the closing chapters the Jews call on him as the one who established his people forever and keeps the temple undefiled, and Judas, recalling the angel sent against Sennacherib, prays for victory and blesses him for manifesting himself and keeping his place undefiled.

l: Demetrius, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Demetrius, a king and son of Seleucus, lands at Tripolis with army and fleet, eliminates Antiochus and Lysias, then is persuaded by Alcimus to send Nicanor against Judas, later ordering Judas sent to Antioch as prisoner.

l: Jason, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jason, brother of Onias, is portrayed as an ungodly, false high priest. He supplants Onias by promising the king silver, builds a gymnasium under the citadel, and pushes his people toward the Greek way of life. Menelaus then outbids him, and he flees as a fugitive to the Ammonites. Later, believing a false rumor of the king's death, he attacks Jerusalem with a thousand men and slaughters his own citizens, yet fails to seize the government. He flees again, is imprisoned by Aretas, hated as a rebel against the laws and pursued from city to city. Seeking shelter among kin Lacedaemonians, he dies in exile, unmourned and unburied.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Judas Maccabaeus is a Jewish military leader, also called Maccabaeus, presented as a noble, trusting commander and the foremost champion of his fellow citizens in body and soul, loyal to them from youth. He is brother to Simon, Joseph and Jonathan. The records open by naming him, with his brothers, as a subject of the history, including the purification of the temple and the dedication of the altar, and note that he gathered the books scattered by the war. He first withdraws with about nine others to the mountains, eating wild plants to avoid defilement. He then secretly gathers about six thousand faithful Jews, trains them, and wins back key positions by night raids. He urges trust in almighty God, divides his army into four parts under himself and his three brothers, defeats Nicanor, and shares the spoils with the maimed, widows, orphans and aged. Led by the Lord, he recovers the temple and city, attacks Idumaean strongholds, executes bribed traitors, prays before facing Timotheus, is guarded by heavenly horsemen, and besieges Gazara. He accepts Lysias's terms out of care for the common good. He avenges the Joppa murders, burns the harbors at Joppa and Jamnia, makes peace and friendship with an Arab army, and takes several towns. At Adullam he leads prayers for the dead and sends two thousand drachmas to Jerusalem for a sin offering, motivated by belief in the resurrection. Camped at Modin, he gives the watchword 'VICTORY IS GOD'S' and leads a night attack on the king's pavilion. Later Alcimus denounces him as leader of the Hasidaeans and Demetrius orders Nicanor to kill him. After a covenant with Nicanor he is urged to marry and settle, but when Nicanor turns harsh he hides and gathers men. In the final account he trusts unceasingly in the Lord, is encouraged by a dream of Onias and Jeremiah, receives a gold sword from Jeremiah, prays, wins, and has Nicanor's head, hand and arm displayed in Jerusalem.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Antiochus is a king (also described as a prince and general) who succeeds Seleucus and rules from Antioch. The records portray him as arrogant, cruel, corruptible, a murderer and blasphemer. Early in his reign he assents to Jason's offer, is received at Jerusalem, then accepts Menelaus's higher bid for the high priesthood. He weeps over Onias's death and executes Andronicus at the place of the crime, yet is persuaded to acquit Menelaus and condemn his three accusers. On his second invasion of Egypt, believing Judea in revolt, he takes Jerusalem by force, orders a massacre, and plunders the temple of 1800 talents with Menelaus as guide, unaware that the Lord's anger over the people's sins was why he succeeded. He appoints governors Philip at Jerusalem, Andronicus at Gerizim and Menelaus, and sends Apollonius with 22,000 men. He then commands the seizure and torture of seven brothers and their mother; the youngest he tries to win with oaths of wealth and honor before treating him worse. The brothers warn of God's judgment. Driven from Persepolis after trying to rob a temple, he vows to make Jerusalem a graveyard, is struck with incurable bowel pain and a fall from his chariot, repents, writes a letter to the Jews, and dies in a strange land among the mountains. Another account has priests killing him by treachery in Nanaea's temple in Persia. His son succeeds him.

l: priests of Nanaea's temple, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: serve_at temple of Nanaea They set out the treasures and, when Antiochus entered with a small company, locked the temple. They opened a secret door in the paneled ceiling, threw stones, struck down the prince, and cut him and his company to pieces by treachery.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jerusalem is the holy city of the Jews, with a citadel and, under Jason, a gymnasium beneath it. It begins in unbroken peace with its laws kept, and its people pray in fear when Heliodorus comes to inspect the treasury, turning to joy after divine intervention. Under Jason's arrangement its inhabitants are to be registered as Antiochenes, and it suffers sacrileges under Lysimachus. Jason assaults it, and Antiochus captures it, slaughtering and enslaving its people and leaving Philip as governor; Apollonius later kills multitudes on the Sabbath. Antiochus first vows to make it a graveyard, then in repentance vows to free it and restore the sanctuary. Lysias plans to settle Greeks there, while Maccabaeus's men draw near.

l: Nehemiah, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Nehemiah is a figure who built the temple and altar in Jerusalem and founded a library of books on kings and prophets. Charged by Persia's king, he sent priests' descendants to find hidden fire; a great blaze followed, and he and companions named the liquid Nephthar, 'Cleansing'.

l: sanctuary in Jerusalem (temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The sanctuary in Jerusalem is the temple, renowned worldwide, called the most holy of all the earth and credited with inviolable sanctity. Its story begins with Solomon's dedication sacrifice, when fire consumed the offerings. Kings honored it with gifts, Seleucus paid for its sacrifices, and Onias cited its sanctity; after the appearance that struck down Heliodorus, terror turned to joy. Antiochus then entered with Menelaus as guide and took vessels and offerings worth eighteen hundred talents. The text says the place was chosen for the nation's sake, so it shares the nation's calamities and benefits. The king ordered it polluted and named for Olympian Zeus; the heathen filled it with debauchery and reveling, and the altar with prohibited things. It is later described as recovered and purified through Judas and his brothers, and promised restoration with all glory at the reconciliation.

l: fire (from the altar), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: was_hidden_by godly priests of that time [in a well without water] It was taken by the godly priests and hidden in a waterless well before the exile to Persia. Later it was found to be thick liquid, which when sprinkled on the sacrifice and exposed to the sun produced a great blaze that consumed the offering. The letter urges the Egyptian Jews to remember it.

l: godly priests of that time, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: hid_fire_before Persia [when fathers were about to be led there] When the fathers were about to be led into Persia, they took some of the altar fire and hid it secretly in the hollow of a dry well. They made sure that no one knew the place.

l: thick liquid (Nephthar), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Nephthar, called Nephthai by most, means Cleansing. A thick liquid found in the well where the fire had been hidden, it was sprinkled by Nehemiah on wood and sacrifices, which blazed in the sun. Poured on stones, it flamed then died. The Persian king enclosed the place and gifted some to favorites.

l: feast of tabernacles, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_kept_in Chislev [month] The Egyptian Jews are told to keep it in the month Chislev in the 188th year. It is linked to the coming celebration of the temple's purification on the twenty-fifth day and to remembering the fire given in Nehemiah's time.

l: purification of the temple, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The purification of the temple is a celebrated event, kept on the twenty-fifth day of Chislev. Jerusalem's Jews announce it to Egyptian Jews, inviting them to keep a feast of tabernacles alongside; the writers urge celebrating the days, credit God with purifying the place, and list it among the history's subjects.

l: Jeremiah, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jeremiah is a prophet of God who prays much for the people and the holy city. He charges the exiles not to forget the Lord's statutes or be led astray by gold and silver images. Warned by God, he hides the tabernacle, ark, and incense altar in a sealed cave, rebuking followers who cannot find it until God shows mercy.

l: Antiochus Eupator, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Antiochus Eupator, son of Antiochus Epiphanes, invades Judea with a huge force, orders Menelaus executed at Beroea, then after a failed Bethsura attack and Philip's recklessness makes peace, honors the sanctuary, appoints Hegemonides, and faces displeasure at Ptolemais.

l: Jason of Cyrene, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: authors Jason of Cyrene's five books Jason of Cyrene is identified as the author who declared the history of Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers in five books. The abridger takes his work as the source to be condensed into one book.

l: abridger (author of the abridgement), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The abridger condenses Jason of Cyrene's five books into one, aiming for brevity to attract readers, aid recall, and benefit all. He describes the labor as sweat and sleeplessness, likens himself to a banquet host and decorator, leaves detail to the original historian, and then begins narrating.

l: cave (Jeremiah's cave), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jeremiah's cave is a hidden place holding the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense, sealed by him; followers later could not find it to mark it, and its location stays unknown until God gathers the people and shows mercy.

l: books (collected by Nehemiah and Judas), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_located with the writers [still with us] Nehemiah, founding a library, gathered the books about the kings and prophets, the writings of David, and letters of kings about sacred gifts. Judas likewise gathered the books scattered by the war, and they are still with the writers, who invite the recipients to send for them if needed.

l: wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and Eupator, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_fought_by Judas Maccabaeus The wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator are listed among the subjects of the history. Heavenly manifestations aided the few who fought bravely for Judaism, letting them seize the country, chase the barbarous multitudes, free the city, and restore the laws.

l: laws of the Jews' fathers (laws of God), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The laws of the Jews' fathers are God-ordained commands given to the fathers through Moses. When the king's envoy tries to force abandonment of Sabbath, feasts and circumcision, Eleazar upholds them as holy and dies rather than violate them, setting an example. Then the brothers, including the youngest, refuse swine's flesh and give body and soul, obeying the law over the king.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The Jews appear as a people chosen by the Lord, bound to laws he ordained, who observe the Sabbath and the feast of weeks, yet who are also described as bound by many sins that turned the Lord's eye away. The records trace their fortunes in a time of persecution and recovery. Early on, they feel indignation at the unjust murder of Onias and appeal to the king, while those who adopted Greek ways are punished by the very men they imitated. Jerusalem's Jews then suffer Jason's slaughter, Antiochus's massacre, enslavement and plundering of the temple, and an attack on the Sabbath, which the narrator attributes to their sins and a brief anger of the Lord. Judas Maccabaeus and a small company escape to the mountains. Persecution deepens: they are forced from their fathers' laws, forbidden the Sabbath, feasts and confessing themselves Jews, made to eat sacrifices and join the Dionysus procession, and many are killed, including women who circumcised their children and people burned in caves for secretly keeping the Sabbath. This is framed as chastening, since God does not forsake his people. Those who stay fight under Maccabaeus, keep the Sabbath, share spoils with the vulnerable, and win victories, and Nicanor admits they are invulnerable when they follow their God's laws. Antiochus threatens to make Jerusalem their graveyard, but after affliction vows to make them equal to Athenians. After lament and prayer they rout Lysias's army with divine help and obtain peace, recognition of rights, and restoration of temple and customs through letters. Conflicts continue at Joppa, Jamnia and elsewhere, with fasting and prayer before battle, a betrayer imprisoned, and the king finally swearing to honor their rights. Divisions appear as some Jews side with Nicanor while others pray, and the elder Razis is hunted. Some compelled to follow Nicanor plead for the Sabbath. After victory the people bless the Lord and decree a yearly commemoration on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Mordecai's day, and the city is held by the Hebrews thereafter.

l: Jason of Cyrene's five books, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: These five books contain the narrative of Judas Maccabaeus, the temple's purification, and the wars. The abridger notes their confusing mass of numbers and abundance of matter, and plans to condense them into one more readable book.

l: Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Onias is Jerusalem's godly high priest, noble, gentle and virtue-trained, who hated wickedness so laws were observed. He disagreed with Simon over the market, protected widows', orphans' and Hyrcanus's deposits from Heliodorus, then sacrificed for Heliodorus's recovery, whose life was granted for his sake.

l: Heliodorus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Heliodorus, chancellor serving King Seleucus, is sent to confiscate the Jerusalem treasury's money despite Onias's explanation. A horse and two young men scourge him, leaving him helpless; spared after Onias's sacrifice, he sacrifices, vows to God, and warns the king that God's power protects that place.

l: Simon, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Simon is a man of the tribe of Benjamin and a guardian of the temple. After disagreeing with Onias over the ruling of the market, he failed to prevail and informed Apollonius of Tarsus that the treasury held untold sums open to the king's seizure; Onias called him impious and false. Later, left by Maccabaeus to besiege two towers, he took a bribe of seventy thousand drachmas and let some enemies escape, so Maccabaeus had him killed as a traitor.

l: Seleucus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Seleucus, king of Asia, pays for the Jerusalem temple's sacrifices from his own revenues, then, informed by Apollonius of the treasury's money, sends Heliodorus to remove it, and is later warned of God's power there.

l: temple (Jerusalem temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The temple is a great and holy sanctuary in Jerusalem whose treasury holds widows' and orphans' deposits, totaling four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. Heliodorus, entering with guards to inspect it, is struck down before taking the money. Foreigners later profane it, and Maccabaeus recovers it, pulls down foreign altars, cleanses it on the twenty-fifth of Chislev (the same day it was profaned), and makes a new altar, restoring sacrifices, incense, lamps and show bread. Nicanor then threatens to level it, and the priests pray that this recently cleansed house stay undefiled forever.

l: deposits (temple treasury), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The temple treasury holds deposits of widows and orphans plus money of Hyrcanus son of Tobias, totaling four hundred silver and two hundred gold talents. Onias explains this; priests and people pray God keep deposits safe. It ends with the treasury kept, not confiscated.

l: horse and rider (apparition), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_trait rider in complete golden armor [horse adorned with beautiful trappings] A horse with a frightening rider, adorned with beautiful trappings, appeared to Heliodorus and his guards near the treasury. The horse rushed fiercely and struck Heliodorus with its forefeet, and the rider seemed to wear complete golden armor.

l: two young men (apparition), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_trait strong, beautiful and splendidly dressed Two young men, notable in strength, beautiful in glory, and splendid in apparel, stood on either side of Heliodorus and scourged him unceasingly with many stripes. They appeared again in the same garments, told him to thank Onias because the Lord granted him life for Onias's sake, and commanded him to proclaim God's sovereign majesty to all. Then they vanished.

l: Heliodorus's scourging and the divine manifestation, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Near the treasury, the Sovereign of spirits caused a manifestation that made Heliodorus's guards faint in terror, while Heliodorus fell to the ground in darkness and was carried out on a stretcher, speechless and hopeless. The event made him recognize God's sovereignty and led to joy in the temple. After Onias's sacrifice he was granted life, and he testified to what he had seen.

l: Simon, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Simon, an informer who earlier gave information about the money against his country, slanders Onias as inciting Heliodorus. His hatred escalates into murders by an approved agent, while Apollonius increases malice. Menelaus is his brother.

l: Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Onias is a high priest, benefactor of the city, guardian of his countrymen and zealot for the laws. He urged the king to secure the people's good, was supplanted by his brother Jason, withdrew to a sanctuary at Daphne, reproved Menelaus for temple theft, and was lured out by Andronicus and killed.

l: Menelaus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Menelaus, brother of Simon, is a corrupt high priest who rises by outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver. He rules as a cruel tyrant: he withholds the promised money, steals temple vessels, has Onias killed after being reproved, and escapes accusation by bribing Ptolemy. He leaves his brother Lysimachus as deputy. When Jason assaults the city, he takes refuge in the citadel, then guides Antiochus into the temple, proving a traitor to the laws and his country. Left as a governor, he is worse than the others. Later, joining the king's expedition and hoping to be set over the government, he encourages Antiochus hypocritically. Lysias blames him for all the evils, and the king has him taken to Beroea and pushed into a tower of ashes, dying without a grave, justly for sinning against the holy altar.

l: Lysimachus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_deputy_of Menelaus [in the high priesthood] Lysimachus, brother of Menelaus, was left as deputy in the high priesthood and committed many sacrileges with Menelaus's consent, including the theft of many gold vessels. When the people rose against him, he armed about three thousand men under Hauran, but the crowd with stones, logs and ashes wounded and killed many of them and killed Lysimachus beside the treasury.

l: Andronicus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Andronicus, a high-ranking man left as the king's deputy, took stolen gold vessels from Menelaus and treacherously murdered Onias after luring him from the sanctuary with oaths and a handshake. The king later stripped him, paraded him through the city, and executed him at the murder site.

l: gymnasium (Jason's gymnasium), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_purpose training of youths [Greek-style] Jason obtained the king's permission to set up a gymnasium and a body of youths trained in it, offering one hundred fifty talents more. He eagerly established it under the citadel itself and had the noblest young men wear the Greek hat. Priests despised the altar and sacrifices and hurried to the wrestling arena after the summons to discus-throwing.

l: Hellenization, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jason immediately shifted his own race to the Greek way of life, setting aside royal ordinances favorable to the Jews and introducing new customs forbidden by the law. The text calls it an extreme of hellenization and an advance of foreign religion. Priests despised their fathers' honors and valued Greek prestige, and the text says calamity followed.

l: high priesthood, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The office was taken from Onias by his brother Jason through a promise of silver, then taken from Jason by Menelaus, who outbid him by three hundred talents. Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as deputy in it. The text calls Jason an ungodly man and not a high priest, and Menelaus kept the office through the covetous dealings of those in power.

l: murder of Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: provokes Jews [also many other nations] At Menelaus's request, Andronicus used treachery, gave Onias his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary at Daphne, and killed him without regard for justice. Jews and many other nations were indignant, and the king wept over Onias's sober and well-ordered life. Andronicus was executed at the very place of the crime, the Lord rendering him the punishment he deserved.

l: Apollonius, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Apollonius, called a lord of pollutions, was sent by Antiochus with twenty-two thousand troops to kill adults and enslave women and boys. He came to Jerusalem feigning peace, waited for the Sabbath, then had armed men parade and slaughtered the onlookers and great multitudes.

l: Jason's assault on Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jason's assault on Jerusalem, triggered by a false rumor of Antiochus's death, saw him rout the wall's defenders with a thousand men and nearly take the city as Menelaus fled to the citadel; he slaughtered citizens, failed to gain government, and fled shamefully to the Ammonites.

l: Antiochus's massacre of Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Believing Judea was in revolt, Antiochus took Jerusalem by force and ordered soldiers to kill everyone in their path, including houses' occupants. Over three days eighty thousand died, forty thousand in close combat, and as many were enslaved; all ages were slain.

l: Eleazar, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Eleazar is a ninety-year-old principal scribe of noble countenance, resolutely loyal to God's laws. Forced to eat swine's flesh, he spits it out and walks willingly to the torture instrument. He refuses his acquaintances' offer to feign eating, fearing to mislead the young and to escape God. He dies under blows, suffering bodily but gladly in soul, leaving an example of virtue.

l: persecution of the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: A persecution ordered by the king, who sends an old man of Athens to force Jews to abandon their laws; a decree extends it to neighboring Greek cities at Ptolemy's suggestion. It brings forced sacrifices, processions, and killings of circumcisers and Sabbath-keepers, interpreted as chastening, not destruction.

l: swine's flesh, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Swine's flesh is food forbidden and abominable to Jews; Eleazar, forced to eat it, spits it out, refusing even pretense, and chooses death over defilement.

l: seven brothers, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Seven brothers and their mother are tortured under the king's compulsion to eat swine's flesh. Loyal to their ancestors' laws, they refuse and die one after another, voicing hope in God's compassion, resurrection and everlasting life, warning the king of judgment; the last hopes their deaths end God's wrath.

l: mother (of the seven brothers), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: A mother, called marvelous and worthy of honorable memory, watches all seven sons die in one day, bearing it courageously through hope in the Lord. She exhorts each in her fathers' language, trusting the Creator to return their spirit and life. Urged by the king, she tells the youngest to accept death, then dies last.

l: first brother (spokesman), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The first brother serves as spokesman for his siblings, declaring they would die rather than break ancestral laws. The king tortures him by cutting out his tongue, scalping him, severing extremities and frying him alive before his family, who urge noble death, trusting God's compassion.

l: youngest brother, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The youngest brother is offered wealth, honor, and friendship by Antiochus if he abandons ancestral ways, but refuses. Loyal to the law given through Moses rather than the king, he warns the king he will not escape God's hands. Treated worse than the others, he dies pure, trusting the Lord and praying for the nation.

l: tortures, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The tortures include scourges and cords, heated pans and caldrons, cutting out the tongue, scalping, and removing extremities, and frying the first brother alive. The second brother has the skin of his head pulled off with the hair, and the third has his tongue and hands demanded. The brothers regard the pains as nothing, the king is astonished, and the chapter closes by referring to them as the extreme tortures.

l: Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Nicanor, son of Patroclus, is a chief friend of the king and former master of the elephants, described as thrice-accursed, boastful and arrogant. In Chapter 8, Ptolemy appoints him to destroy the Jews and sell captives to raise the king's two-thousand-talent tribute to the Romans; his army is routed and he flees to Antioch, admitting the Jews have One who fights for them. In Chapter 14, as governor of Judea appointed by Demetrius, he is sent to kill Judas but instead befriends him, then, after the king's rebuke, plots against him, threatens the temple, and sends soldiers against Razis. In Chapter 15 he resolves to attack on the Sabbath, claims to be a sovereign on earth, and advances with trumpets and victory songs. He is found dead in full armor; his head, hand and arm are taken to Jerusalem and displayed.

l: Maccabaeus's army, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_size six thousand [at gathering] About six thousand men are gathered, trained and divided into four parts, three of them led by his brothers with one thousand five hundred men each. They kill more than nine thousand of Nicanor's force, wound and disable most of the rest, and rout them. Afterward they kill more than twenty thousand of Timotheus's and Bacchides's forces, take high strongholds, and store captured weapons in strategic positions.

l: Gorgias, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Gorgias is an accursed, war-experienced captain and governor of Idumaea who keeps mercenaries to fight the Jews. He rides out with infantry and cavalry, is nearly captured by Dositheus, escapes wounded to Marisa, and his troops are routed by Judas.

l: Timotheus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Timotheus is a governor of a district who refused to let the Jews live in peace. Previously beaten, he gathered large foreign forces and Asian cavalry, commanding 120,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry, but they fled in terror before Judas. He sent his family and baggage to Carnion, tricked Dositheus and Sosipater into freeing him, then was found hidden in a cistern at Gazara and killed.

l: Seleucid army (Nicanor's forces), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_size twenty thousand [at least, of all nations] Nicanor's army consists of no fewer than twenty thousand men of all nations, joined by the experienced captain Gorgias. More than nine thousand are killed, most of the rest are wounded or disabled, and all are compelled to flee. The army is destroyed.

l: battle with Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_outcome victory for the Jews [Nicanor's army fled] Eleazer reads aloud the sacred book, gives the watchword 'THE HELP OF GOD', and leads the first band to join battle with Nicanor. Because the Almighty fights on their side, the Jews kill more than nine thousand enemies and put the rest to flight. They stop the pursuit because the Sabbath is near, and they take the money of the merchants who had come to buy them as slaves.

l: Antiochus's illness, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_inflicted_by God [fatal and invisible stroke] An incurable pain of the bowels with bitter inner torments seizes Antiochus as he finishes his boast, which the text calls just for the torments he had inflicted on others. It worsens after his chariot fall into worms, falling flesh and an intolerable stench, until he is broken in spirit and dies.

l: Antiochus's letter to the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: A letter by Antiochus, written as a supplication to the Jews after he gave up hope for himself; it greets them, announces his son Antiochus as king following his father's precedent, and urges continued goodwill.

l: Antiochus (son of Antiochus), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_successor_of Antiochus [appointed king] The king's son Antiochus is appointed king in the letter, which says the father often entrusted and commended him to most of the Jews. The father is persuaded that the son will follow his purpose and treat them with moderation and kindness, and Philip fears him after the king's death.

l: Maccabaeus's men, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: follow Maccabaeus [company] Maccabaeus' men tore down foreign altars, cleansed the sanctuary, and offered sacrifices anew. They fought the Idumaeans and Timotheus, and after four days at Gazara, some young men among them assaulted the wall, burned the towers, and opened the gates to take the city. They then blessed the Lord with hymns.

l: rededication festival (eight days), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: An eight-day rededication festival kept with gladness like the feast of tabernacles, recalling wandering in mountains and caves like wild animals. People carried leafy wands, branches and palms and sang thanksgiving hymns; a public decree ordained yearly national observance.

l: Lysias, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Lysias is the king's guardian, kinsman and chancellor, later appointed supreme governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia by Eupator. He first marched against the Jews with a huge army, intending to Hellenize Jerusalem and profit from the temple, and besieged Bethsuron. After a shameful flight, he recognized the Almighty fought for the Hebrews, negotiated terms, and wrote the Jews promising to advocate for them. Later he accompanied Antiochus Eupator, blamed Menelaus for the evils, and at Ptolemais defended the treaty, pacifying the angry people before departing to Antioch.

l: Idumaeans, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The Idumaeans, masters of key strongholds, harassed the Jews with Gorgias and sheltered Jerusalem refugees; Maccabaeus's men, after prayer, stormed them, killing over twenty thousand and later capturing two towers holding nine thousand fugitives.

l: bribe (seventy thousand drachmas), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Seventy thousand drachmas were paid by some in the Idumaean towers to Simon and his men. In return, some of the besieged were let slip away. Maccabaeus learned of it and executed the men for betraying their kindred.

l: Timotheus' foreign forces, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Timotheus's army consisted of great multitudes of foreign troops and a considerable Asian cavalry. Driven by passion, they were blinded and thrown into confusion by the heavenly horsemen and cut to pieces. Twenty thousand five hundred were slain, besides six hundred cavalry.

l: five heavenly horsemen, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Five splendid horsemen with golden bridles appeared from heaven as the battle intensified. Two led the Jews and shielded Maccabaeus with their armor, while shooting arrows and thunderbolts that blinded and confused the enemy.

l: Gazara, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Gazara is a very strong fortress commanded by Chaereas, where Timotheus fled. Its defenders trusted its strength and blasphemed through a four-day siege; on day five young men scaled the wall, burned the towers, and Jews took the city.

l: battle with Timotheus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_outcome victory for Maccabaeus [20,500 foot and 600 cavalry slain] After the Jews prayed in sackcloth and dirt before the altar, they advanced from the city and met Timotheus's army at dawn. The Jews relied on refuge in the Lord, while the enemy was led by passion. Heavenly horsemen intervened, and the enemy was thrown into confusion with over twenty thousand slain.

l: King Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: King Antiochus, son of the previous Antiochus, is a ruler who restores Jewish religious freedom. Following his father's wish to leave subjects undisturbed, he writes to his brother Lysias and the Jewish senate, restoring the temple, permitting ancestral laws and foods, granting amnesty, and sending Menelaus.

l: Lysias's army, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_size about eighty thousand infantry plus cavalry and eighty elephants Lysias's army numbered about eighty thousand infantry, all his cavalry, and eighty elephants, and he was puffed up by its size. It lost eleven thousand infantry and one thousand six hundred cavalry to the Jews, and the rest fled, mostly wounded and naked.

l: Battle at Bethsuron, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_outcome Jewish victory [Lysias's army fled] Lysias besieged Bethsuron, a strong place about five stadia from Jerusalem, and Maccabaeus's men advanced against him with the apparition of a white-clad horseman at their head. They fell on the enemy like lions, killing eleven thousand infantry and one thousand six hundred cavalry and putting the rest to flight, Lysias among them.

l: peace terms and royal letters, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: After the defeat, Lysias agreed to terms recognizing the Jews' rights, and Maccabaeus accepted them. Letters follow from Lysias (dated year 148, Dioscorinthius 24), from King Antiochus to Lysias and to the Jewish senate (year 148, Xanthicus 15), and from the Roman ambassadors Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, who consented to Lysias's grants and asked the Jews to send someone promptly about matters referred to the king.

l: men of Joppa, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: The men of Joppa, a group, treacherously drowned at least two hundred Jews after inviting them onto boats, an act called great impiety; Judas retaliated by burning their harbor and boats, killing fugitives, and vowing to return.

l: Jamnites, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jamnites, people of Jamnia, planned harm to neighboring Jews as Joppa had; Judas attacked at night, burning their harbor and fleet, visible from Jerusalem.

l: Caspin, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Caspin was a strong, walled, fortified city with a mixed population beside a two-furlong lake. Its people trusted their defenses and blasphemed against Judas's company; Judas invoked God and captured it in a slaughter that made the lake seem bloody.

l: idol tokens of Jamnia, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Consecrated idol tokens of Jamnia, forbidden to Jews by Law, were found under the garments of each dead Jewish soldier collected at Adullam, and all understood they caused the men's deaths.

l: sin offering for the dead, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Judas collected two thousand silver drachmas man by man and sent them to Jerusalem for a sin sacrifice, so the dead might be released from sin; the text calls this holy and godly.

l: resurrection, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_basis_of prayer for the dead The text says Judas acted well and honorably in taking thought for the resurrection when he sent the offering. It argues that praying for the dead would be superfluous and idle if he did not expect the fallen to rise again.

l: fallen Jewish soldiers, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Jewish soldiers fell fighting Gorgias; gathering bodies for ancestral tombs, Judas's men found Jamnian idol tokens under their garments, prayed for the sin's blotting out, and sent an offering to Jerusalem.

l: Bethsura, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: is_a strong fortress of the Jews Bethsura was a strong Jewish fortress that the king attacked; he advanced, was turned back, failed, and was defeated. Judas sent necessary supplies to those inside, and the king later negotiated with them a second time, giving his hand and taking theirs.

l: king's army (Antiochus Eupator's army), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Antiochus Eupator's army, led by Antiochus and Lysias, was vast: 110,000 infantry, 5,300 cavalry, 22 elephants and 300 scythed chariots each. Judas's night raid killed about 2,000, felled the lead elephant and spread terror; it was later turned back at Bethsura.

l: Judas's company, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: opposes Nicanor's company [enemy in battle] Judas's company is encouraged by his words and the dream, and resolves to bear down on the enemy and settle the matter hand to hand, fearing most for the sanctuary. They join battle with invocation and prayer, kill no less than thirty-five thousand, and return rejoicing, finding Nicanor dead.

l: night attack on the king's pavilion, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Judas led a chosen force of the bravest young men against the king's pavilion by night, using the watchword "VICTORY IS GOD'S". They killed about two thousand men and felled the leading elephant and its rider, terrifying the army, then withdrew successfully at dawn, credited to the Lord's protection.

l: peace treaty between Antiochus and the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: A peace treaty in which the king, hearing Philip grew reckless in Antioch, swore to uphold all Jewish rights, sacrificed, and honored the sanctuary. He appointed Hegemonides governor. Ptolemais's men, indignant, wanted it annulled, but Lysias persuaded and pacified them.

l: Alcimus, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Alcimus, a former high priest called wicked, opposes Judas Maccabaeus. He brings Demetrius gifts and accuses Judas and the Hasidaeans of sedition, is to be installed as high priest, then falsely claims Nicanor is disloyal for naming Judas successor.

l: Razis, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: Razis, a Jerusalem elder, is well reported and called Father of the Jews for his good will toward countrymen, having earlier risked life for Jewish religion. When Nicanor sends five hundred soldiers to seize him, he violently kills himself, calling on the Lord of life.

l: covenants (between Nicanor and Judas), The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_state annulled by king's order [Demetrius was displeased and Nicanor was commanded to send Judas prisoner] After pledges are exchanged and the troops agree, a meeting is held with armed men posted by Judas as a precaution, and the covenants are made. Alcimus takes possession of them and uses them to accuse Nicanor, so Demetrius is displeased and orders Judas sent as a prisoner. Nicanor is troubled at annulling the articles, since Judas had done no wrong.

l: battle between Judas and Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees
s: has_outcome victory for Judas's company [about 35,000 enemy killed and Nicanor dead] The armies join battle with Nicanor's troops set in array, elephants at a convenient post and cavalry on the flanks. Nicanor's side advances with trumpets and songs while Judas's side fights with prayer, killing no less than thirty-five thousand men. The battle ends with Nicanor found dead in full armor.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon
s: This document is a nineteen-chapter wisdom text that exhorts rulers to righteousness, contrasts the fates of the righteous and the ungodly, praises Wisdom, and recounts how she acted in sacred history. It opens by addressing the judges of the earth, urging them to love righteousness and warning that Wisdom will not enter an evil soul. God did not make death; the ungodly summon it. Chapters 2 to 5 give the reasoning of the ungodly, who think life brief and ending in oblivion, so they revel, oppress the poor and plot against the righteous man who calls himself God's child. The narrator replies that God created man for incorruption. The righteous are held in God's hand, tested like gold, and given authority, while the ungodly and their children are punished. Virtue, even in childlessness or early death, brings immortality. In the end the ungodly see the righteous man vindicated and lament, and creation fights for the Lord against his enemies. Chapters 6 to 9 turn to kings and rulers, who are warned that judgment will fall on those who fail to judge rightly, and are urged to seek Wisdom. A speaking king says he is mortal like everyone, prayed for understanding and valued Wisdom above thrones and riches. He describes her as a spirit, a breath of God's power and an image of his goodness. He seeks her as a bride, expecting counsel, honor and immortality, and then prays that God will send her to guide him, since without her no one counts for anything. Chapters 10 to 12 and 16 to 19 retell the story of God's people. Wisdom saved the righteous from the first father through the flood, the burning cities, the dungeon and the exodus, led them across the Red sea, and brought water from rock. The enemies, by contrast, were punished through the very things they worshiped: blood-filled rivers, vermin, locusts, flies, storms, and a heavy darkness, while God's people received quails, bread from heaven, healing and a pillar of fire. A death at midnight struck the oppressors, and a blameless man stopped wrath among the righteous. The pursuing Egyptians met a strange death at the sea. Throughout, God is shown as merciful, loving all things, correcting sinners gradually so they may repent, and judging in gentleness. Chapters 13 to 15 condemn idolatry: nature-worshipers are barely excused, while makers of idols, such as the woodcutter and potter, are ridiculed for praying to lifeless things. Idolatry is traced to grief and royal flattery and called the beginning, cause and end of every evil. The text closes with creation reordering itself like the notes of a lute, and God glorifying his people at every time and place.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: God is presented in these records as the Sovereign Lord of all, the creator and sustainer of the world, whose spirit fills it and who sees every person's inmost self and hears every utterance. He is found by those who do not test him and is manifested to those who trust him. He did not make death and takes no delight in the perishing of the living; he made all things so they might have being, and made humanity for incorruption, in the image of his own everlastingness. The early chapters center on the contrast between the righteous and the ungodly. God holds the righteous in his hand, tests them like gold, accepts them, crowns them, and shows grace and mercy to his chosen and holy ones. He shields them with his right hand and arm. The ungodly he laughs to scorn. He takes up zeal, righteousness, impartial judgment, and holiness as armor and uses creation as a weapon to punish his enemies. The middle chapters turn to rulers and wisdom. God is the source of kings' dominion, will search out their works, and shows no deference to greatness, since he made and cares for small and great alike. He guides and corrects even wisdom, loves the one who dwells with her, and must be the one to give wisdom. The speaker addresses him as God of the ancestors and Lord of mercy, who made all things by his word and formed humankind by his wisdom, who chose the speaker as king and commanded a sanctuary on his holy mountain, and who is asked to send Wisdom and his holy spirit. Later chapters stress his gentle, forbearing justice: his incorruptible spirit is in all things, he rules righteously, his strength is the source of righteousness, and he gives sinners repentance. The closing chapters recount his dealings with his people, whom he calls his sons, with covenants and oaths to their fathers and a holy land. He guided them with a pillar of fire, destroyed the Egyptians' army in a flood, foreknew the ungodly's change of mind, remade creation to keep his servants unharmed, and delivered them. The record ends with him magnifying and glorifying his people, standing by their side in every time and place.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Wisdom is presented as a personified spirit who loves humanity yet will not enter a soul that devises evil or a body enslaved by sin, and who does not hold a blasphemer guiltless. The records open by setting this moral condition for her presence, then turn to how she is found. She is radiant and unfading, easily seen by those who love her, and she anticipates and graciously meets those who seek her and are worthy. Her beginning is desire for instruction, which leads to love, observance of her laws, immortality and a kingdom. Envy has no fellowship with her. The middle of the records describes her nature. She is the architect of all things, a pure and subtle spirit more mobile than any motion, a breath of God's power, a reflection of everlasting light, and fairer than the sun. Though one, she can do all things and renews them while remaining in herself. She passes into holy souls to make them friends of God and prophets, and evil does not prevail against her. The narrator prefers her to thrones, riches, gems, health and beauty, since all good came with her, and he sees her as a bride, counselor and companion who must be given by God. Her relation to God is central. She lives with him, is loved by him, sits by him on his thrones, knows his works, and was present at creation. She understands what pleases him, chooses his works, and teaches soberness, understanding, righteousness and courage. She knows the past and foresees the future. A prayer asks God to send her from the heavens to work with and guide the speaker. The final movement is a historical sequence of rescue. Wisdom guards, delivers, guides and prospers the righteous, beginning with the first formed father, whom she delivers from his transgression and strengthens to rule. She saves a righteous man in the flood, preserves another blameless, delivers one from the fire on the five cities, guides a fugitive in straight paths and shows him God's kingdom, and goes with a sold and imprisoned man into the dungeon and gives him eternal glory. She delivers the holy people from oppressors, enters a servant of the Lord, leads the people through the Red sea, drowns their enemies, and gives speech to the mute and to babes. The records close by noting she prospered the works of the righteous through a holy prophet, framing the desert journey that follows.

l: judges of the earth, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_exhorted_to love righteousness The judges of the earth are directly addressed and commanded to love righteousness, to think of the Lord with a good mind, and to seek him in singleness of heart. They are also warned to beware of unprofitable murmuring and slander, and not to court death or draw destruction on themselves by the works of their hands.

l: the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The ungodly are a group who neglect righteousness and revolt from the Lord. In Chapter 1, their words and hands summon death, and they make a covenant with him, deeming him a friend. In Chapter 3, they are punished as their reasoning deserves; their hope is void, their toils and works useless, and their families foolish and cursed. In Chapter 4, they watch the wise man's end without grasping the Lord's plan, then become a dishonored carcass, are left waste, and their memory perishes.

l: death, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Death is presented as not made by God, who delights not in the perishing of the living; Hades holds no royal dominion on earth. The ungodly summon death, befriend it, and treat it as a final, irreversible end. The narrator counters that God made man for incorruption, and death entered through the devil's envy, afflicting his own.

l: righteousness, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is immortal Righteousness is declared immortal. The judges of the earth are urged to love it, and it stands in contrast with the ungodly, who summon death.

l: creation, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Creation is portrayed as God's obedient servant, wholesome and free of destructive poison. In Chapter 5 the whole creation becomes the Lord's weapon, fighting alongside him against his frenzied foes, with sea and rivers overwhelming the wicked. In Chapter 19 it is made new, each part in its kind, complying with God's commands to keep his servants unharmed. Like lute notes changing rhythm, elements swap roles: land and water creatures exchange habitats, fire persists in water, and flames spare creatures and food.

l: the ungodly (those who speak in verses 1-20), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The ungodly are a group who hold that life is brief, chance-born, and ends in oblivion. Reasoning thus, they pursue hedonistic revelry and oppress the righteous poor, while plotting against the righteous man who reproaches their sins, testing whether God will save him. The narrator says they are blinded by wickedness, ignorant of God's mysteries, and belong to the devil.

l: the righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The righteous man professes knowledge of God, calls God his father, and lives a way of life unlike others', avoiding the ways of the ungodly as uncleanness. Because he reproaches their sins, they plot to torment him, test him with insult and torture, and condemn him to a shameful death to see whether God will deliver him. In the end he stands boldly before his afflicters, who are terrified and amazed at his salvation, and admit he is counted among the sons of God and has a lot among the saints.

l: man (humanity created by God), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Humankind was formed by God's wisdom to rule creatures and the world in holiness and righteousness. Mortals have unstable thoughts, fragile plans and a burdensome corruptible body, and cannot grasp heavenly things; yet wisdom corrected their ways, taught them what pleases God, and saved them.

l: enjoyment of pleasures (hedonistic revelry), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: includes costly wine and perfumes The ungodly urge one another to enjoy the good things that exist, filling themselves with costly wine and perfumes, crowning themselves with rosebuds, and leaving tokens of mirth everywhere, since this is their portion and lot. This revelry is paired with their resolve to oppress the righteous and is part of the reasoning the narrator calls unsound.

l: the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The righteous are held in God's hand, tested and found worthy. Though seeming dead, they rest in peace with hope of immortality. After brief chastening they receive great good, judge and rule nations, and live with God in love, understanding truth.

l: parents of unlawfully conceived children, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Children of adulterers, born of unlawful unions, are portrayed as doomed: they will not reach maturity and their seed vanishes. If they live long, their old age lacks honor; if they die young, they have no hope or consolation on judgment day.

l: immortality, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Immortality is kin to wisdom and brings closeness to God; in Chapter 8 the speaker expects it, plus eternal memory for posterity, through wisdom, so he seeks her.

l: virtue, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Virtue, per Chapter 4, makes childlessness better than a large family: its memory grants immortality and is recognized before God and men. It is imitated when present, longed for when gone, and marches crowned, victorious in contests for undefiled prizes.

l: brood of the ungodly (offspring), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The multiplying brood of the ungodly, their illegitimate offshoots, profits nothing. Like branches that flourish briefly, they are shaken and uprooted by winds, broken off before maturity, bearing useless, unripe fruit. Unlawfully conceived children finally witness against their parents's wickedness when investigated.

l: righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The righteous man is found well-pleasing to God and loved, and is taken from among sinners so evil cannot corrupt his understanding or soul. Even dying early he is at rest, perfected quickly, and in death condemns the living ungodly.

l: honorable old age, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Honorable old age, per Chapter 4, is measured not by length of time or years but by understanding, likened to gray hair, and an unspotted life.

l: final judgment of the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A judgment scene for the ungodly: they arrive in coward fear as their sins are counted, and their lawless deeds convict them to their face. The Lord then dashes them speechless down, leaves them waste and anguished, their memory perishing, a dishonored carcass in lasting reproach.

l: early death of the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The early death of a righteous man is framed as rest, not loss: he was taken lest wickedness corrupt him. His soul pleased the Lord, so he hurried from wickedness. The peoples miss this, but it condemns the long-lived unrighteous.

l: those who afflicted the righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The afflicters of the righteous man, seeing him, are seized with terrible fear and groan in repentance. They confess they derided him as mad, strayed from truth, and traveled lawless, destructive paths ignorant of the Lord's way; their arrogance and riches profited nothing, and wickedness consumed them.

l: the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The righteous live forever with their reward in the Lord and the Most High's care; they receive the royal crown and beautiful diadem from his hand, covered and shielded by his right hand and arm.

l: the ungodly's fleeting prosperity, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The ungodly's fleeting prosperity: in Chapter 5 the wicked confess that their arrogance, riches and boasting vanished like a shadow, rumor, wake, bird's path or arrow, leaving no trace; their hope is likened to chaff, foam, smoke, and a one-day guest's memory.

l: divine armor (the Lord's armor), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Lord's divine armor, taken from his zeal: righteousness as breastplate, impartial judgment as helmet, invincible holiness as shield, and sharpened stern wrath as sword.

l: storms and elements (weapons against the wicked), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A storm event in which the Lord's creation arms itself against the wicked: lightning flies true, hailstones are hurled, sea and rivers overwhelm them, and a mighty wind winnows them away, leaving the land desolate.

l: kings and rulers (the addressees), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Kings, judges, rulers and princes, addressed as officers of God's kingdom, are told their dominion came from the Lord, yet they failed to judge rightly or keep the law. They face stern, swift judgment, and are urged to learn wisdom and honor her to reign forever.

l: judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: has_quality stern [on those in high places] Judgment is said to come awfully and swiftly, and sternly, upon those in high places because the rulers did not judge rightly or keep the law. The lowly may be pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested, and scrutiny of the powerful is strict. Those who kept holy things in holiness and were taught them will find what to say in defense.

l: speaker (the king, son of God's handmaid), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The speaker is a king who presents himself as an ordinary mortal, formed in his mother's womb and descended from the first-formed man, weak and short-lived, and a servant of God and son of God's handmaid. He prayed and received understanding and a spirit of wisdom, choosing her over sceptres, thrones, riches, health and beauty, and gained knowledge of the natural world. He shares wisdom freely. Chosen by God as king and judge of his people, and commanded to build a sanctuary and altar, he asks for Wisdom so he may judge righteously and be worthy of his father's throne.

l: one formed first (first-formed man), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_a man created alone He was created alone and was guarded to the end by wisdom. She delivered him out of his own transgression and gave him strength to rule over all things.

l: knowledge of the natural world, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The narrator says God gave him unerring knowledge of the structure of the universe and the operation of the elements. This covers the beginning, middle and end of times, solstices and seasons, the circuits of years, the positions of stars, living creatures, wild beasts, winds, the thoughts of men, plants and the virtues of roots. He says he learned all things secret or manifest because wisdom, the architect of all things, taught him.

l: mortality and common human birth, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: applies_to mankind [one entrance into life and a common departure] The narrator describes himself as a descendant of the first-formed man, formed as flesh over ten months in his mother's womb, born drawing the common air and uttering the same first cry as everyone. He was nursed in swaddling clothes, and he concludes that no king had a different beginning, since all men share one entrance into life and a common departure.

l: the speaker (narrator), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A first-person speaker who has loved wisdom since youth and sought her as a bride, expecting counsel, comfort, glory, honor, rule, and immortality. Describing himself as a clever child with a good soul and undefiled body, he concludes wisdom must be given by God, and so prays to the Lord wholeheartedly.

l: God's people (Israel, your sons), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: God's people, called his servants, children, and 'your sons', belong to God even when they sin, because they know his dominion and trust him. They are heirs of the Lord's oaths and covenants made with their fathers, and are taught that the righteous must be kind and that God gives sinners repentance. When chastened, they are to ponder his goodness and look for mercy, while their enemies are scourged far more. They were not led astray by idol worship, though oppressed by idol-worshiping enemies. In the wilderness they receive quails and angels' food, are healed by God's word, and are troubled only briefly by beasts and serpents, with a token of salvation recalling the law. They are guided by a pillar of fire, glorified by the same means that punish their enemies, and as holy children secretly offer sacrifice and agree to the covenant of the divine law, sharing good things and perils. They also suffer death in the wilderness, though the wrath is brief.

l: unrighteous man (who killed his brother), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: An unrighteous man abandons wisdom in anger, kills his brother, and perishes himself in the same rage.

l: righteous man (saved by wood in the flood), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: When the earth was drowning with a flood for the sake of the unrighteous man, wisdom saved it by guiding this righteous man's course by a paltry piece of wood.

l: righteous man (loved his child), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: When nations consenting together in wickedness were confounded, wisdom knew this righteous man and preserved him blameless to God. She kept him strong when his heart yearned toward his child.

l: righteous man (fled the fire on the five cities), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Wisdom delivered him while the ungodly perished, as he fled from the fire that descended out of heaven on the five cities.

l: five cities, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Five cities destroyed by fire from heaven for wickedness; their ruin endures as memorials: a smoking waste, fair fruit that never ripens, and a standing pillar of salt.

l: righteous man (fugitive from his brother's wrath), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Wisdom guided him in straight paths while he fled his brother's wrath. She showed him God's kingdom, gave him knowledge of holy things, prospered his toils, stood by him against covetous men and enemies, and judged his severe conflict so that he would know godliness is more powerful than everyone.

l: righteous man (sold, imprisoned, then made ruler), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: receives sceptre of a kingdom [from wisdom, with authority over his tyrants] He was sold, but wisdom did not forsake him and delivered him from sin. She went down with him into the dungeon and stayed with him in bonds until she brought him a kingdom's sceptre and authority over his tyrants, showed his mocking accusers to be false, and gave him eternal glory.

l: holy people, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A holy people, a blameless seed, delivered by Wisdom from oppressors; she rewarded their toils, guided and sheltered them by day and night, brought them across the Red sea, and they sang praise to God's holy name.

l: nation of oppressors, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: This nation oppressed the holy people and blameless seed, from whom wisdom delivered them. Its enemies were drowned and cast up from the bottom of the deep, and the righteous plundered the ungodly.

l: servant of the Lord, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: withstands terrible kings [through wonders and signs, by wisdom] Wisdom entered into the soul of this servant of the Lord. He withstood terrible kings in wonders and signs.

l: Red sea, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Red sea is a body of water where wisdom brought the holy people through much water and drowned their enemies, casting them up from the deep. It then yielded an unhindered dry highway and grassy plain, letting God's people pass over.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: God is portrayed as the Sovereign Lord, creator of the world out of formless matter, who arranges all things by measure, number, and weight and possesses great strength at all times. The records stress his mercy: because he can do all things, he has mercy on humanity, loves everything he made, abhors none of it, and overlooks sins so people may repent. He is called gracious, true, patient, Savior of all, architect and first author of beauty, and is more powerful than the elements and heavenly bodies people worship; mankind can perceive their Maker from the greatness of creation. The account unfolds from creation and character toward his dealings in history. He treats the Israelites, his children, as a father admonishing them, and the Egyptians as a stern king condemning the ungodly. He gives the righteous water from flinty rock, quails, and bread from heaven, while punishing their foes with blood in the river and irrational creatures. He guides sailors and saved mankind's seed on a raft when proud giants perished, and he will punish the deed together with the doer. He molded man, breathing in an active soul and vital spirit, heals by his word, holds authority over life and death, and cannot be escaped. Creation serves him, strengthening against the unrighteous and slackening for those who trust him.

l: Israelites (the righteous), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The righteous Israelites crossed a barren desert, withstood enemies, and when thirsty called on God and received water from the rock; chastened in mercy, they learned how the ungodly were tormented in wrath.

l: Egyptians (the ungodly enemies), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Egyptians, ungodly enemies, worshiped irrational reptiles and vermin through senseless imaginings, so God sent such creatures to punish them, judging them with wrath. Their river turned to clotted blood for the decree to slay babies; distressed, they heard others benefited, recognized the Lord, and marveled at their unusual thirst.

l: water from the rock, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: comes_from flinty rock [healing of thirst] Water was given from flinty, hard stone to the righteous when they thirsted and called on God, providing healing of their thirst. It was given abundantly and beyond hope, and it stood in contrast to the river turned to clotted blood, showing that the same things that punished foes benefited the righteous in need.

l: irrational creatures (reptiles and vermin), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The ungodly were led astray to worship irrational reptiles and wretched vermin in their senseless imaginings. In return, God sent upon them a multitude of irrational creatures as punishment, though the text says he could equally have sent bears, lions, or newly created fire-breathing beasts.

l: divine mercy, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: extends_to men (humanity) [all men] God's mercy extends to all men because he has power to do all things, and he overlooks human sins so that they may repent. The text grounds this in his love for all that exists, his abhorrence of nothing he made, and his sparing of all things because they are his. The righteous were chastened in mercy, and the ungodly were not destroyed outright by a single breath.

l: sin and punishment, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: has_principle a man is punished by the things by which he sins The chapter teaches that by what things a man sins, by these he is punished, as shown by the worship of reptiles being answered with creatures sent against the worshipers. Justice could have scattered the sinners by a breath, yet God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, and punished the ungodly as a king while admonishing the righteous as a father.

l: old inhabitants of your holy land, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Former inhabitants of the holy land, hated by God for detestable practices including enchantments, unholy rites, child slaughter, and sacrificial banquets of human flesh and blood. Though counsel was to destroy them, God spared them, sent hornets, and judged them gradually to allow repentance, knowing their inborn evil would not change: a cursed seed from the beginning.

l: holy land, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: has_attribute most precious of all lands [in God's sight] The holy land is called most precious of all in the Lord's sight. Its old inhabitants were destroyed so that it might receive a worthy colony of God's servants.

l: Egyptians, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Egyptians are portrayed as ungodly oppressors who refused to know God and enslaved his people, the holy ones and children of God, along with guest benefactors whom they hated. Their punishment is presented as deserved and fitting. They are afflicted by vermin, locusts and flies, then by strange rains, hail, storms and fire, and are imprisoned in darkness, losing sight. After plotting to kill the holy ones' babes, they lose their children and whole army in a flood. Terrified by dreams, and having disbelieved because of enchantments, they confess the people to be God's children. They then foolishly pursue those they had driven out, meeting a strange death.

l: unrighteous who lived in folly, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: An unrighteous, foolish people who worshipped animals even their enemies despised, deceived like foolish babes. The Lord first sent mocking judgment as to children, then tormented them through their own abominations; punished by their supposed gods, they recognized the true God, followed by extreme condemnation.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Divine judgment is righteous and unchallengeable by any king, prince or avenger. Though God could act at once, he proceeds gently and gradually, giving chance to repent: mild correction and mockery first, then deserved, extreme condemnation for the unheeding. It models how God's people should judge.

l: repentance and forbearance, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: teaches God's people (Israel, your sons) [model of kindness for the righteous] The Lord's forbearance is shown in judging offenders little by little, giving times and opportunities to escape wickedness, even to the old inhabitants of the land whose nature he knew would not change. It is rooted in his strength and sovereignty, and it teaches his people to be kind and gives them good hope because he gives repentance when men sin. Those who refuse mild correction eventually face the deserved judgment.

l: men who had no perception of God, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Men with no perception of God are called foolish by nature: they failed to know the Sovereign Lord from the good things seen or recognize the architect from his works. They took fire, wind, stars, or water for gods. Seekers swayed by beauty earn small blame yet no excuse; worshipers of handmade things are miserable, hoping in dead things.

l: nature worship (fire, wind, air, stars, water, luminaries), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_a belief that elements are gods ruling the world Fire, wind, swift air, circling stars, raging water, and luminaries of heaven were taken to be gods that rule the world. The text says that if people admired their beauty or power, they should instead recognize how much better and more powerful their Maker is.

l: idols (works of men's hands), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Idols are hand-made objects of gold, silver, stone, or carved wood, formed from things God created. They are lifeless, weak, and unable to move or help themselves, so they must be secured in a wall with iron; their hands have no ability. They are accursed together with their makers, an abomination, a stumbling block and snare to the foolish. They did not exist from the beginning and will not last, having entered the world through human boastfulness, so a speedy end was planned and a visitation is coming upon them.

l: woodcutter, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A woodcutter fells a tree, strips it, makes a useful vessel for life's needs, and burns the scraps to cook and eat. From a discarded crooked, knotty piece he idly carves an idol, paints it red, fixes it in a wall with iron, and shamelessly prays to it for goods, marriage, children, health, journey, and profit.

l: idolatry, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: has_hopes_in dead things [practitioners are miserable] Idolatry is depicted as praying to a lifeless object for goods, marriage, children, health, life, aid, a good journey, and success in business. The text shows its absurdity by noting that the one addressed is dead, weak, and unable to move, and must be secured by its maker so it won't fall.

l: wood, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Wood is a fragile material, more fragile than a sailor's vessel, yet under God's guidance it brings sailors and rafts safely to land, including the raft of the world's hope; blessed when bringing righteousness, accursed as an idol.

l: idolatry, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Idolatry is presented as the worship of images, hateful to God along with the ungodly. It began with a grieving father honoring his dead child's image, then hardened into custom and law by princes' commands, and spread through flattery of distant kings and an artisan's beautified likeness. Calamity and tyranny led people to name stones and stocks divine. It is called the beginning of fornication and of every evil.

l: worshipers, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Idol worshipers are described as straying from knowledge of God, living in ignorant war yet calling evils peace. They practice madness, lying prophecy, unrighteousness and false oaths, trusting lifeless idols for safety, and because they thought evil of God and despised holiness, just judgment will pursue them.

l: moral corruption, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: includes murder, theft, deceit, perjury, adultery [fills all things] The chapter lists the consequences of idolatry as slaughtering children in rites, frenzied revels, treacherous killing, adultery, blood and murder, theft, deceit, faithlessness, tumult and perjury. It also names ingratitude, defiling of souls, confusion of sex and disorder in marriage, so that neither life nor purity of marriage is guarded.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Divine judgment is just: it punishes the idol maker together with the deed, announced as a visitation among the nation's idols, and ends by declaring that the sinners' just penalty, not the power of what they swore by, overtakes the unrighteous who swore falsely.

l: potter, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The potter is a maker of clay vessels who kneads earth and shapes them for clean and contrary uses, judging each one's purpose. He also molds a vain god from the same clay to an evil end. Though made of earth and soon to return the lent soul, he is ignorant of his Maker, has a heart of ashes, treats life as a profit game, and sins beyond all others.

l: idols, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Idols are lifeless objects made by mortal hands from earth, lacking eyes, nostrils, ears, fingers, and feet. Enemies of God's people and the nations consider them gods. Their maker surpasses them, having lived while they never did, and their painted forms lead fools into lust.

l: enemies of God's people, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A group oppressing God's people, called most foolish and more miserable than a baby because they deem the nations' idols gods, though those idols cannot see, breathe, hear, handle, or walk.

l: idol worship, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Idol worship is condemned as deception: painted images of dead, breathless forms lead fools into lust.
