Makers, desirers, and worshipers are called lovers of evil things, deserving such hopes, and they even venerate the most hateful, senseless creatures, unbeautiful and outside God's praise and blessing.

l: vermin, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: torments enemies (oppressors of God's people) A multitude of vermin, like the creatures the oppressors worship, are sent to torment them. Their hideousness makes the oppressors loathe even necessary appetite.

l: quails, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Quails are a delicacy God sends to satisfy his people's appetite, given in place of the vermin punishment inflicted on their enemies.

l: angels' food (bread from heaven), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Angels' food is ready-to-eat bread from heaven, given by God without toil; it holds every pleasant flavor, suits every taste, and shifts to each eater's choice, showing God's sweetness toward his children.

l: storms of hail, rain and fire, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Strange rains, hails and relentless fire-storms punish the oppressors of God's people. Fire burns hotter in water, sometimes restraining itself to spare creatures, destroys an unrighteous land's produce, yet forgets its power to nourish the righteous while snow and ice endure it.

l: lawless men, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Undisciplined lawless men who strayed believed they held a holy nation in their power, yet became prisoners of darkness, exiled from eternal providence and divided by forgetfulness. Their magic and understanding failed, ordinary sounds terrified them, and all, laborers included, were bound by one chain of night.

l: holy nation, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The holy nation is the group the lawless men supposed they held in their power. It is not described as suffering the darkness; the whole world, by contrast, was illuminated with clear light and unhindered works while the darkness lay over the lawless men alone.

l: darkness, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_a image of the darkness that should afterward receive them [heavy night over them alone] The darkness is a heavy, long night that holds the lawless men like a prison not barred with iron. No fire or star could illuminate it, and it came out of the recesses of Hades. It was spread over them alone and is called an image of the darkness that should afterward receive them, though to themselves they were heavier than darkness.

l: God's judgments, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: God's judgments are great and hard to interpret, leading undisciplined souls astray; the chapter shows this through darkness imposed on lawless men as an inescapable sentence all endured.

l: fear, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_a surrender of the help which reason offers Fear fills the lawless men through phantoms, terrifying sounds, vermin, and serpents, so that they perished trembling and refused even to look at the air. The text defines fear as a surrender of the help which reason offers, and says wickedness, condemned by conscience, is cowardly and always forecasts the worst. Even natural sounds such as wind, birds, water, rocks, and beasts paralyzed them with terror.

l: firstborn children (Egyptians' children), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Egyptians' most cherished offspring were consumed at a single stroke, leaving corpses without number, too many for the living to bury. Their destruction led the Egyptians to confess the people to be God's children.

l: death of the firstborn, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: A deadly night strike on Egypt's firstborn, delivered by God's word like a sharp-sworded warrior at midnight in silence. It killed servant and master, commoner and king alike; preceding dreams and fears explained the deaths, and Egyptians confessed the people as God's children.

l: wilderness plague, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: touches holy ones (God's people) [multitude destroyed in the wilderness; wrath short-lived] Death also touched the righteous in the wilderness, and a multitude were destroyed, but the wrath did not last long. Dead had fallen in heaps before the blameless man intervened, stopped it, and cut off its way to the living.

l: blameless man (Aaron), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: Aaron, a blameless servant of God, is shown as high priest whose ministry uses prayer and atoning incense. He hurries to defend the people and halts the wilderness plague by his word, recalling the fathers' oaths and covenants. His robe, stones, and diadem picture the world, the fathers' glories, and God's majesty.

l: destroyer, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: yields_to blameless man (Aaron) [feared the robe, stones and diadem] The destroyer, called the avenger, was subdued by the blameless man's word and the remembrance of the covenants. It yielded and feared his robe, stones and diadem, since it was enough only to test the wrath.

l: God's people (Israelites), The Wisdom of Solomon
s: is_covered_by God [covered with God's hand] God's people journeyed on a marvelous road, overshadowed by the cloud and covered by God's hand, and passed over with all their army having seen strange marvels. They roamed like horses and skipped like lambs, praising the Lord who delivered them. They remembered the lice and frogs of their sojourning and saw a new kind of bird, quails from the sea, when they desired luxurious dainties.

l: Egyptian pursuit of the Israelites, The Wisdom of Solomon
s: The Egyptians, after eagerly sending the Israelites away, changed their minds and pursued them while still mourning, a foolish decision. Foreknown by God, it was drawn on by deserved doom to complete their punishment and bring a strange death, while his people traveled a marvelous road.

l: The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: This is the Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), a 51-chapter wisdom book of instruction, mostly addressed to 'my son'. Its central theme is that all wisdom comes from the Lord and that the fear of the Lord is its beginning, fullness, crown and root. Chapter 1 sets this out, and later chapters return to it repeatedly, including the claim that nothing surpasses fear of the Lord. The first and largest part is a collection of maxims and counsels. They urge patience, trust and endurance in testing, since gold is tried in fire. They cover honoring parents, humility, almsgiving and care for the poor, and strict discipline of children and slaves. They treat friendship, warning against false friends and self-interested advisers and praising the faithful friend, and they deal with prudent speech, with warnings against the double tongue, gossip, whispering and betrayed secrets. They also address caution toward the powerful and rich, lending and surety, moderation at table and with wine, health and sorrow, women and wives (the good wife praised, the wicked or unfaithful one condemned), the contrast of the wise man and the fool, and warnings against pride, sin and presuming on God's mercy. Chapters 15 to 17 stress that the Lord left man free to choose between life and death and that he rewards deeds yet accepts repentance. Chapter 24 is a high point in which Wisdom praises herself, comes to dwell in Israel and Jerusalem, and is identified with the law of Moses. Later chapters include a prayer for Israel and against foreign nations (36), honor for the physician and the scribe over the craftsman (38), reflections on the toil of all humanity and on death (40 and 41), and a hymn to creation's wonders (43). The final section, chapters 44 to 50, is a praise of famous ancestors. It names Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, the judges, Samuel, Nathan, David, Solomon (whose bowing to women led to a divided kingdom), Elijah, Elisha, Hezekiah, Isaiah, Josiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the twelve prophets, Zerubbabel, Jesus son of Josedek, Nehemiah, and Adam. It culminates in the high priest Simon son of Onias and his temple liturgy. The author then closes with a prayer for Israel and signs as Jesus, son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem, blessing whoever lays the book up in his heart. Chapter 51 ends with thanksgiving for rescue from death, slander and enemies, and with the author's account of seeking wisdom from youth. He invites the uneducated to her house of instruction, to take her yoke without money, and to do their work before the Lord gives their reward.

l: the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord, also called the Most High, God, and the Holy One, is the central deity of these records from The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach. He is the source and creator of wisdom, who sits on his throne, is greatly to be feared, and gives wisdom freely to those who love him and keep his commandments. He is creator and maker of all things, humankind (from earth), the universe, and the wise man; he is everlasting, needs no counselor, is greater than all his works, upholds all things by his word, and is unseen. His works are wonderful, hidden, and unfathomable. What matters most is the pairing of mercy and judgment. He is full of compassion, forgives sins, multiplies forgiveness, saves in affliction, and has mercy on all flesh like a shepherd. He is also a just judge with no partiality, who cannot be bribed. He hates sinners, abomination, and the deceitful schemer, and takes vengeance on the vengeful. He repays everyone according to deeds, and he crushes the unmerciful. He commands no one to be ungodly and gives no license to sin. He holds the government of the earth in his hand, raises up and casts down rulers, uproots and overthrows nations, and is the source of riches and poverty, life and death. He sees all, searches the heart, and declares past and future. He honors the father and confirms the mother's judgment, and he curses whoever provokes the mother. He hears the poor, the wronged, the fatherless, and the widow, accepts the humble, and is glorified by the lowly. He protects, delivers, and is the hope of those who fear him, and fear of him is wisdom. The records unfold from wisdom and trust in him, through his dealings with the proud, sinners, nations, and mankind, to his covenant and law of life for mankind and his creative power in nature. They close with his acts in Israel's history. He glorifies Moses and gives him commandments face to face, exalts Aaron with an everlasting covenant, destroys Dathan and Abiram with fire, and makes a covenant with David. He watches over Jacob, preserves a remnant, and never forsakes his mercy. Finally, the Holy One hears the people and delivers them by Isaiah, as his angel destroys the Assyrian camp.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Wisdom is a personified, feminine figure in the Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach. She comes from the Lord, is with him forever, and was created before all things and before the ages, coming out of the mouth of the Most High. She is given freely to those who love the Lord and is tied to keeping the commandments. Her duration is eternal, and no first or last man has fully explored her; her thoughts are filled from the great deep. The records show her relationship to seekers as demanding but rewarding. She exalts her sons, takes hold of those who seek her, and is loved by the Lord. She first walks with a follower in crooked ways, bringing fear, dread and discipline until she trusts his soul. Then she returns him to the straight way and reveals her secrets, but she forsakes and hands over to his fall anyone who goes astray. She is harsh to the unlearned and like a mighty stone of trial to those without understanding, and she is manifest to few. For those who persevere, her fetters become a covering of strength, a robe of glory and a crown of rejoicing, and she yields rest and gladness at the last. She can be gathered from youth and found with gray hair, and cultivating her takes little toil before her fruit is eaten. She is also pictured as a house with windows, doors, walls and branches, offering shelter from heat, good things and glory. For the one who fears the Lord she is like a mother and a wife, feeding him bread of understanding and water of wisdom, exalting him above his neighbors and opening his mouth in the congregation. She is far from pride and is not obtained by foolish men, sinners and liars. The account culminates in her self-praise. After seeking rest among all peoples, she was told by the Creator to dwell in Jacob and take her inheritance in Israel. She ministered in the holy tabernacle before the Most High, was established in Zion, and was given rest in Jerusalem, rooted in the honored people, the Lord's own portion. She compares herself to cedar, cypress, palm, olive, plane, cinnamon, myrrh, terebinth and vine, and to rose bushes in Jericho. Her memory is sweeter than honey. Her stream grew from a canal into a river and then a sea, watering the garden, and she labors not for herself only but for all who seek wisdom.

l: fear of the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The fear of the Lord is presented in Sirach as the foundation and summit of wisdom: its beginning, fullness, crown, and root. It is glory, exultation, gladness, and a crown of rejoicing, giving joy, length of days, peace, perfect health, and a blessed end. Chapter 1 warns against disobeying it or approaching the Lord with a double heart, and says deceitful people lacking it will be cast down. Chapter 23 shows those left behind learning that nothing is better or sweeter than it, alongside heeding the commandments. Chapter 25 calls it the glory of the aged, surpassing all things, with no one greater than one who holds it.

l: those who love the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Those who love and fear the Lord are a group described as honored, blessed, and greater than any prince, judge, or mighty man. They keep his ways, are filled with the law, and obtain wisdom, relying on her without being moved. The records open with their honor in contrast to commandment-breakers. They then show them inheriting joy, a crown of gladness, and an everlasting name. They end living in spirit, unafraid, with the Lord's eyes as protection, raising their souls and giving health, life, and blessing.

l: praise of God's creation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A topic of praise for the Lord's creation: all his works are exceedingly good, visible to his eyes, and each serves its purpose and is approved in its time, so none should be questioned or called worse. It then turns to exhortation, urging people to look at the rainbow, praise its maker, and exalt the Lord with full strength, though no praise suffices and many greater works remain hidden.

l: My son, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: My son is the addressee of instruction: if he comes to serve the Lord, he must prepare his soul for temptation, set his heart aright, endure, cling to the Lord, accept hardship, be patient in humiliation, trust, and make his ways straight.

l: those who fear the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Those who fear the Lord are people marked by obedience and humility. They do not disobey his words, seek his good pleasure, prepare their hearts, and humble their souls before him. Chapter 2 calls them to wait for his mercy and trust him, hoping for eternal gladness. Chapter 32 adds that they receive discipline, find favor and true judgment, kindle righteous acts like a light, and suffer no loss.

l: temptation, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Temptation is what the one who comes to serve the Lord must prepare his soul for. It is likened to the testing of gold in fire and of acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.

l: patience, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Patience is urged when suffering humiliation, together with constant endurance and not making haste in calamity. Those who have lost their patience receive a woe and are asked what they will do when the Lord visits them.

l: trust in the Lord, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Trust in the Lord is a topic in Chapter 2: it brings the Lord's help and an unfailing reward for those who fear him, since no one trusting him was ashamed.

l: the faint-hearted and fearful, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The faint-hearted and fearful are a group pronounced under woe in Chapter 2; because they do not believe, they will not be defended.

l: divine mercy and wrath, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord's mercy and wrath are held together and proportioned to his majesty. Chapter 2 urges fearers to wait and hope for his great mercy, preferring his hands to men's. Chapter 16 adds that he forgives yet pours out wrath, correction matches mercy, and the godly's perseverance will not be frustrated.

l: the law, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: fills one who seeks it He who seeks the law will be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble at it. He who believes the law gives heed to the commandment.

l: father, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A father acts as instructor, calling his children to hear and obey. He is a source of glory through honor given him; his blessing establishes his children's houses. He must be honored, helped in old age, and patiently tolerated; forsaking him is blasphemy.

l: mother, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_attribute curse roots out foundations The mother's judgment over her sons is confirmed by the Lord, and one who gives her glory is as one who lays up treasure. Her curse roots out the foundations of a house. One who provokes her is cursed by the Lord, and a mother in dishonor is a reproach to her children.

l: children (the speaker's children), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The speaker's children are addressed as those who must hear and do what they hear so that they may all be safe. The father's blessing establishes their houses, while the mother's curse uproots the foundations. A mother in dishonor is a reproach to them.

l: son (the addressed son), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The son is told to help his father in old age, not to grieve him, and to be patient if he fails in understanding. He is also told to go on with his business in humility, to humble himself more the greater he is, and not to seek things too hard for him or beyond his strength. He is urged to think about what has been commanded him, since he has no need of the secret things.

l: honoring parents, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Honoring parents is a teaching on filial duty in Chapter 3. It promises atonement for sins, length of days, joy in children, and answered prayer, likens giving glory to mother to laying up treasure, says kindness to a father is remembered in affliction, and urges serving parents without dishonor.

l: humility, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Humility is commended in Chapter 3: practiced even in daily business, it brings love from an acceptable man and favor before the Lord; the greater one is, the more he should humble himself, since the Lord is glorified by the lowly.

l: pride and stubbornness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Pride and stubbornness are warned against in Chapter 3: conceit leads many astray, a stubborn heart ends badly and is burdened with troubles, and the proud suffer incurable calamity because wickedness has taken root, with sin heaped upon sins.

l: the poor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_owed generosity to the poor [should not be deprived of living or made to wait] The poor, needy, hungry and afflicted are those the son must not deprive, delay, provoke, reject or turn away from. If a poor man curses in bitterness of soul, the one who made him will hear his supplication. The son is to incline his ear, answer him with peaceful words, and deliver him from anyone who wrongs him.

l: son (the addressee), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The son is the addressee of instructions in Chapter 4: give promptly to the poor, defend the wronged, and act as father to the fatherless, so he becomes a son of the Most High. He is also told to seek wisdom, speak truth, confess sins, and be consistent.

l: those who seek wisdom, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Those who seek wisdom early are filled with gladness, serve the Holy One, and are loved by the Lord. They inherit glory and security if they trust her through discipline and testing; those who stray are forsaken to their fall.

l: generosity to the poor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_commanded_by son (the addressee) [don't turn away from one who asks] Generosity to the poor is commanded as giving without delay, without turning one's face or eye away, and without giving occasion for a curse. It includes humble, peaceful words, rescuing the wronged, and caring for the fatherless and their mother, and it brings the reward of being as a son of the Most High. The chapter closes by warning against a hand that is stretched out to receive but closed when it should repay.

l: sinner (who has a double tongue), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A sinner with a double tongue, who habitually winnows with every wind and walks every path; he receives evil condemnation and bears a reputation of shame and reproach, like a thief.

l: reader (addressee), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_commanded_to_be steadfast in understanding [instruction] The reader is told not to set his heart on goods or unrighteous gains, not to follow his own mind and strength, and not to presume on the Lord's patience or on atonement. He is told not to put off turning to the Lord, to be steadfast and consistent in speech, to be swift to hear and patient in answering, to answer his neighbor if he has understanding or otherwise put his hand over his mouth, and not to be ignorant in any matter.

l: sin, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Sin is treated as something one must not minimize by asking what happened after sinning, or compound by adding sin upon sins out of confidence in atonement. Sinners face the Lord's indignation, and unrighteous gains will profit nothing in the day of calamity.

l: speech and the tongue, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Speech and the tongue are presented as a double-edged power: they hold both glory and dishonor and may cause a man's downfall. Chapter 5 urges consistency, patient answers or silence, and avoiding whispering, ambush, and double-tongued speech. Chapter 20 warns that much talk breeds hatred, a tongue's slip is worse than a fall on pavement, and wise speech wins love and favor.

l: whisperer, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The whisperer, called double-tongued and a disreputable title to avoid, is a slanderer to be cursed: he destroyed many at peace, dispersed them among nations, toppled strong cities and great houses, and cast out brave women.

l: faithful friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A faithful friend is described as a strong defense, a treasure, and life-saving medicine, priceless with nothing exchangeable for him. Those who fear the Lord find him, and such a person directs friendship properly, since his neighbor will be as he is.

l: friendship, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Friendship is counseled to grow through sweet words and a gracious tongue, which multiply friends; peaceful relations should be many, advisers rare, and friends gained by testing, not hurried trust, directed by fear of the Lord.

l: false friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A false friend is a fair-weather companion described in Chapter 6: friendly only for an occasion, a table companion who fails in affliction, or one who becomes an enemy and exposes strife to your reproach. In prosperity he acts as an equal and bold over servants; when you are brought low he turns against you and hides. The text advises separating from enemies and being wary of friends.

l: my son (the addressee), The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A son, the addressee, receives counsel in Chapter 6: gather instruction from youth, pursue wisdom like a farmer and bear her yoke, listen willingly, stand among elders, attach to the wise, meditate on the Lord's commandments, avoid self-exaltation, and test friends before trusting.

l: priests, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Priests serve as ministers of the Lord and are to be revered and not forsaken. Chapter 7 instructs honoring them by giving their commanded portions: first fruits, trespass offering, shoulders, sanctification sacrifice, and first fruits of holy things.

l: servant, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A servant, owed liberty if wise, is given bread, discipline and work. Kept busy to prevent idleness and escape; an evil one faces yoke, whip and fetters, yet is treated like oneself, bought with blood, and may flee if ill treated.

l: evil and unrighteousness, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Evil and unrighteousness are portrayed as bringing punishment: avoiding evil keeps it from overtaking a person, while sowing unrighteousness reaps sevenfold. The chapter ends with the ungodly facing fire and the worm, and wrath not delaying for sinners.

l: almsgiving and charity, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Almsgiving and charity is a commanded duty: alms must not be neglected, and stretching a hand to the poor completes one's blessing. The teaching widens to not avoiding weepers, mourning with mourners, visiting the sick to gain love, and giving gifts with grace, even toward the dead.

l: mighty man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_warned_against contending with him [risk of falling into his hands] The mighty man is someone one should not contend with, lest one fall into his hands. Lending to a man stronger than oneself is advised against, and if one does lend, it should be counted as a loss.

l: rich man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_disposition overpowers those who strive with him [risk when striven with] The rich man is someone one should not strive with, lest he overpower the person. The text notes that gold has destroyed many and turned away the hearts of kings.

l: the wise, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The wise are a group whose discourse and proverbs should not be neglected; learning them teaches discipline and how to serve great men, as Chapter 8 urges.

l: sons of Adam, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The sons of Adam, humanity collectively, bear a heavy yoke and great travail from birth until burial in the earth, troubled by fear of the future and death; one is warned against confiding in him.

l: riches, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Riches are portrayed as dangerous: they destroy many, turn kings' hearts away, and cause wakefulness and anxiety that consume the flesh. Love of gold is a stumbling block leading fools to ruin, leaving its lover unjustified.

l: practical wisdom and prudent conduct toward others, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: advises avoiding conflict with the powerful The unit presents prudent conduct as avoiding quarrels with powerful, rich, loud, wrathful, reckless, or foolish people, and as showing humility and compassion toward those who repent, the old, and the dead. It also advises caution in lending, giving surety, going to law with a judge, and revealing secrets or one's heart, while learning from the wise and aged to gain understanding and an answer in time of need.

l: death, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Death is presented as a universal, inevitable decree that will not wait. It is the covenant from the beginning over all flesh, 'You must die!', and the sentence of the Most High, whose good pleasure it is. Generations pass like leaves and works rot with their builders. Death falls on every creature, sevenfold on sinners, and the fear of it troubles everyone from king to poor. Reactions differ: it is bitter in memory to a prosperous man at peace, but acceptable to a needy, failing, very old man. The text concludes it should be accepted rather than feared, since no one asks about life in Hades however long it lasted.

l: woman, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_effect leads many astray by her beauty [passion kindled like a fire] Women appear as potential dangers to a man: the wife should not be given cause for jealousy or an evil lesson, and a woman can trample a man's strength if he gives her his soul. Prostitutes, singers, and married women are described as snares and tricks, and a woman's beauty is said to have led many astray, kindling passion like a fire. A man is told not to dine or revel with a woman who has a husband, lest he slide into destruction.

l: old friend, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_not_comparable_to new friend [should not be forsaken] The old friend is not to be forsaken, because a new friend is not comparable to him. The text likens a new friend to new wine, which one will drink with gladness once it has become old.

l: law of the Most High, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The law of the Most High belongs to the Lord and is bound up with wisdom. Transgressing it makes even the clever worse than God-fearing simple people, while the wise man meditates on it, glories in the Lord's covenant law, and shows its instruction.

l: avoiding sexual temptation from women, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A topic of instruction on avoiding sexual temptation from women. It begins with advice to turn the eye from a beautiful woman and not dine with a married one, then lists Chapter 9's commands against prostitutes, singers, virgins and wandering streets, warning of snares, lost inheritance, penalties and destruction.

l: choosing good companions, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Advice on choosing good companions: know your neighbors, take counsel with the wise, converse with men of understanding about the law of the Most High, and dine with righteous people. It closes with warnings to avoid men with power to kill and not to envy sinners.

l: pride, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Pride is hated by the Lord and by men. It starts when a man's heart departs from his maker, its beginning is sin, and whoever keeps it pours out abomination; it was not created for men.

l: judge, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A judge whose character shapes his officials: a wise judge instructs his people and his officials mirror him; though honored, he is ultimately lesser than one who fears the Lord.

l: king, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A king, described in Chapter 10, whose lack of discipline destroys his people and who, being mortal, will die tomorrow like everyone else.

l: rulers, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord cast down the thrones of rulers and set the lowly in their place. As a city's ruler is, so are all who dwell in it, and the government of the earth is in the Lord's hand.

l: nations, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: undergo_transfer_of sovereignty [because of injustice, violence, and greed for money] Sovereignty is transferred from nation to nation because of injustice, violence, and greed for money. The Lord plucked up the roots of nations, overthrew their lands to the foundations of the earth, and made the memory of some of them cease.

l: the lowly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: are_set_in_place_of rulers [by the Lord] The Lord planted the lowly in the place of the nations whose roots he plucked up. He also set them on the thrones of the rulers he cast down.

l: scribe, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The scribe receives honor from the Lord and gains wisdom through leisure; with little business he can become wise, unlike busy laborers who cannot.

l: physician, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The physician is a healer created by the Lord, honored for his skill, which wins admiration from great men and gifts from the king. Though long disease mocks him, the sick are urged to keep him near, since recovery sometimes lies in his hands, and he himself asks the Lord to prosper diagnosis and healing.

l: humility and honor, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: advised_to my son [glorify your soul in humility] The son is told to glorify his soul in humility and to ascribe to himself honor according to his worthiness. Honor should not go to a sinner, nor be withheld from a poor man with understanding. The text prefers the man who labors and abounds over the one who boasts and lacks bread, and says a poor man is honored for knowledge while a rich man is honored for riches.

l: the lowly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: has_attribute wisdom [lifts their head and seats them among great men] The wisdom of the lowly lifts up his head and seats him among great men, just as the little bee produces the best of confections. One who was never thought of has worn a crown, and the Lord raised up a poor, weak man from his low condition so that many marveled at him.

l: the godly, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The Lord's gift remains with the godly, and his good pleasure toward them will prosper forever. His blessing is in their reward, and he makes it flourish in an hour that comes swiftly.

l: proud and deceitful man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: A proud, deceitful man is portrayed as a decoy partridge and a spy seeking weakness. He lies in wait, turning good into evil, blaming praiseworthy things, and plotting bloodshed through many tricks. The reader is warned not to bring such a man into the house, since his wicked schemes could ruin one's reputation.

l: riches and poverty, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Riches and poverty are said to come from the Lord. One may grow rich by diligence and self-denial yet not know how soon he will leave his goods to others at death. The Lord can swiftly make a poor man rich, and a man should not say he has enough or that he lacks any further good.

l: hasty speech and meddling, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_discouraged_for son [meddling brings punishment] The text counsels against blaming before investigating, answering before hearing, interrupting a speaker, and arguing about matters that do not concern one. It warns that busyness over many matters and meddling bring punishment, and that one who toils and hurries can still fall further behind.

l: godly man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: is_recipient_of almsgiving and doing good [should be given to] The godly man is the one the reader is told to do good to and to give to. Doing good to him brings a reward, if not from him then from the Most High.

l: sinner, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The sinner is portrayed as someone who should receive no almsgiving or help, since aiding him invites double harm. The Most High hates and avenges sinners. He stays with associates only while things go well and abandons them when they falter, so joining him earns no pity.

l: enemy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The enemy is a deceitful figure whose wickedness is like corrosion in copper. He is not hidden in adversity, where he waits, grieves at prosperity, speaks sweetly and weeps while plotting a pit, seeks blood given opportunity, feigns help to trip the reader, and mocks. He should be kept away, lest he take the reader's place.

l: almsgiving, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Almsgiving is a recurring theme of charitable giving, presented as a commanded act of keeping the Most High's commandments and glorifying the Lord with generosity, equivalent to a thank offering. Early, it is to be given knowingly to the godly and lowly, earning thanks and reward, and withheld from sinners and the ungodly. Next, it is said to profit more than gold and, stored up, to deliver from affliction and fight enemies better than shield or spear. Finally, it endures forever and rescues in affliction better than relatives and helpers.

l: distrust of the enemy, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Chapter 12 counsels permanent distrust of an enemy: stay careful even when he humbles himself, like someone polishing a mirror to stop tarnish. Never seat him beside you or at your right hand, lest he overthrow you; ignoring this leads to regret.

l: rich man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The rich man is portrayed as an exploitative, deceptive figure who wrongs others and threatens when at fault. He uses those who are profitable, drains the owners of resources, smiles falsely, then forsakes and mocks those he has stripped. He preys on the poor, who are an abomination to him. When he falls, many helpers rally; when he speaks, all keep silent and praise him. His riches are good only if sinless.

l: poor man, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: The poor man is a figure of social contempt: he apologizes when wronged, is preyed upon and despised by the rich, and is abandoned by friends in need. When he falls he is rebuked and pushed aside; his wisdom is ignored and he is dismissed with 'Who is this?' Poverty is evil only in the ungodly's opinion.

l: fellowship with the powerful, The Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus
s: Chapter 13 warns against fellowship with the proud, mighty, or rich, using images like pitch, pots, wolf and lamb, hyena and dog. Such ties bring exploitation, deception, and abandonment. If a mighty man invites you, stay reserved, neither pressing nor distant, don't speak as equals, distrust his words, guard secrets; creatures keep to their own kind.
